newsitem.title: UK: POLL-UK inflation to stick to gov't target in June.
newsitem.headline: POLL-UK inflation to stick to gov't target in June.

text.p: Underlying British inflation will remain glued to the government's 2.5 percent target in May although headline prices will edge up, economists forecast.
A Reuter poll of economists found a consensus that figures out at 0830 GMT on Tuesday would show retail prices rose 0.2 percent last month, leaving them 2.8 percent higher than a year earlier.
But RPIX, which excludes volatile mortgage interest payments, is expected to stay put at 2.5 percent year-on-year.

It is those home loan payments that will have forced up the headline rate, as Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's decision to raise base rates after just five days in office forced mortgage lenders to raise their rates.

"The increase in mortgage interest rates at the start of the month should have pushed the headline inflation rate higher during June, despite a beneficial movement in the underlying figure," said David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders.
Most mortgage lenders raised their rates by 0.35 percentage points in response to a quarter-point base rate rise on May 6.

Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets, said the upward pressure from mortgage rates would be partially offset by utilities prices. He agreed with the consensus forecast of a 0.2 percent rise in the RPI over the month but said the markets would focus firmly on core retail prices.
"Goods inflation will be particularly closely watched upon the start of the summer sales, with a further rise in clothing and footwear inflation likely to renew fears of widening margins."
But he said that was unlikely to happen while a significant rise in households goods inflation in June last year should lead to a year-on-year fall in Tuesday's figures.
Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, forecast the annual rate of underlying retail price inflation edged down to 2.4 percent in June as the pound's strength started to exert itself.
"Sterling strength is expected to continue to feed through to retail goods inflation, most especially food, this month," he said.
The pound has leapt by about 20 percent on a trade-weighted basis since last August. Last month, the Office for National Statistics said seasonal food prices tend to rise in June.
Figures out on Monday showed British manufacturing output slumped by 1.1 percent in June, the largest monthly fall since 1993. Analysts said the pound's strength was the main culprit there too.
But few expected those figures, or Tuesday's inflation data, to stop the Bank of England tightening monetary policy soon, and maybe as soon as Thursday after its monetary committee meets.

"The Bank of England are looking at inflation in 12-18 months time and those pressures are coming from the services sector and not the manufacturing sector," said Andrew Milligan, economist at General Accident.
